content_html:
Ecosystem Beyond Plants and Animals

An ecosystem is a system of relations among living (biotic) and non‑living (abiotic) components. Plants, animals, and humans are only part of the whole. Microbes, fungi, soils, water, air, climate, and energy flows are equally fundamental. Cooperation and resilience emerge from these multi‑layered interactions.

An ecosystem is not just plants supporting animals. It is a system of primary production, consumption, decomposition and nutrient cycling, embedded within and dependent on abiotic processes.

The underlying model has five components:

  1. Sunlight and climate provide environmental conditions and energy.
  2. Plants are primary producers, converting solar energy into organic matter.
  3. Animals consume organic matter and contribute to pollination, seed dispersal and other ecological interactions.
  4. Fungi and microbes decompose organic material, recycle nutrients and interact with the soil matrix.
  5. Water and atmosphere are abiotic systems participating in the exchange and cycling of matter.

This view echoes Buddhist interdependence and systems theory: no component is isolated; meaning and function emerge from relations. Consciousness (in some animals, especially humans) is one kind of emergent property, but cooperation does not require awareness — microbes and fungi “cooperate” structurally through cycles and symbioses.

Biotic Components

  • Plants: capture solar energy; structure habitats; mediate carbon/water fluxes.
  • Animals: consumers, dispersers, engineers; include insects, fish, birds, mammals, humans.
  • Fungi: decomposers, mutualists (mycorrhizae), pathogens; central to soil fertility and plant health.
  • Microorganisms: bacteria, archaea, protists; drive nutrient cycles (nitrogen fixation, decomposition, fermentation).

Abiotic Components

  • Soil: mineral matrix + organic matter + microbes; stores water and nutrients; ecological “memory bank.”
  • Water: freshwater and marine systems; solvent, habitat, and energy transporter.
  • Air: atmosphere mediates climate, dispersal of seeds/pollen, gas exchange.
  • Climate & disturbance: temperature, rainfall, storms, fire; set disturbance regimes and renewal cycles.
  • Energy & geochemistry: sunlight, heat, carbon/nitrogen/phosphorus flows structure system dynamics.

Interactions & Emergence

  • Feedback loops: Microbial decomposition releases nutrients → plants grow → animals feed → waste/death feeds microbes again.
  • Resilience: Soil legacies, microbial seed banks, and cultural practices buffer disturbance.
  • Panarchy: Local microbial shifts scale up; regional climate memory scales down, aligning the whole.

References

  • Ecological systems definition: Tansley (1935). ++The use and abuse of vegetational concepts and terms++. Ecology.
  • Role of microbes & fungi: van der Heijden, M. G. A., et al. (2008). ++The unseen majority: soil microbes as drivers of plant diversity++. Nature.
  • Soil as memory: Johnstone et al. (2016). ++Ecological memory and forest resilience++.
  • Trophic cascades: Estes et al. (2011). ++Trophic downgrading of planet Earth++. PNAS.
